prompt:
## Background & Goal You are evaluating a terminal Markdown renderer (Renderer A) against CommonMark spec examples. Renderer B is shown alongside as a reference comparison. The goal: assess whether Renderer A produces a good terminal experience for a human reader. Is the content readable? Is the structure clear? Does the ANSI styling help or hinder? Terminal ANSI is limited compared to HTML — bold, dim, color, underline, strikethrough are the main tools, and layout is also limited. Judge human-readable experience, not byte-for-byte HTML equivalence. ## Step 1: Feature weight (0.0–1.0) Rate the Markdown feature being tested — the input itself. Is this a foundational pattern people use daily, or obscure spec trivia? Consider real-world frequency in documents, AI output, READMEs, chat. 1.0 — ubiquitous, almost every document has this 0.9 0.8 0.7 — common in typical usage 0.6 0.5 — appears occasionally 0.4 0.3 — infrequent, niche use 0.2 0.1 — extremely rare, almost never encountered in practice ## Step 2: Score both renderers (0–3) 0 — Content lost (full or partial), garbled, altered, or unreadable. 1 — Content is preserved and readable, but structure is lost or presented in a misleading way. 2 — Content and structure are clear. Different parts of the document are visually distinguishable. Structure can be conveyed through line breaks, indentation, prefixes, or ANSI styling — different approaches can serve the same purpose well. Style may be basic but does not mislead. 3 — Content, structure, and style all work well together. Styling choices are appropriate and enhance readability. Note: if the input itself has no structure (e.g. a single word), there is nothing to distinguish — score 2 or 3 may be the best possible rendering if content is preserved and nothing is misrepresented. Important: Score is independent from weight. Weight determines the pass/fail threshold only — do not use weight to adjust the score itself. Because ANSI is limited, a renderer may add extra prefixes or markers (e.g. `#` for headings) to help convey structure — this is not a content failure. Also, a renderer may represent structure differently than HTML would (e.g. indentation vs nesting). Different but effective is good. ## Reference example Markdown input: # Title A paragraph with **bold** text. Expected HTML:

Title

A paragraph with bold text.

Weight: 1.0 — headings and emphasis are ubiquitous. Score 0 → "" (empty or garbage) Score 1 → "Title A paragraph with bold text." All text present but flat — heading runs into paragraph, no structure. Score 2 → "Title\n\nA paragraph with bold text." Heading on its own line with blank line — structure is clear. Bold not styled but content and organization are visible. Score 3 → bold-yellow "Title" + "\n\n" + "A paragraph with " + bold "bold" + " text." Heading distinguished by style, bold rendered as bold. Content, structure, and style all present. ## Additional considerations The notes below add expectations specific to this example (e.g. "HTML tags are stripped — content is still preserved"). These supplement the general 0–3 scale. ## Example to evaluate __SECTION_NOTES__ Markdown: __MARKDOWN__ Expected HTML: __HTML__ Renderer A: __MDFLOW_OUTPUT__ Renderer B: __GLOW_OUTPUT__ ## Output format Return ONLY valid JSON: { "weight": 0.0-1.0, "weight_explanation": "one or two sentences", "a_score": 0-3, "b_score": 0-3, "issues": ["if any"], "explanation": "brief justification" }
